strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and useful task formulation—transferring a full temporally-evolving effect from a reference video onto a separate input video/image (Ref + Input -> Output)—that is meaningfully different from prior static-reference or text-prompt-based editing paradigms.

Substantial engineering effort in constructing a large, diverse training corpus (>120K triplets, >1,700 effects) from three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V, a novel automated V2V pipeline using first-last-frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects), addressing the key bottleneck that video-to-video effect triplets do not naturally exist.

The proposed scalable V2V pipeline (image editing -> pose extraction -> conditional video generation) is a reasonable and creative solution to a genuinely hard data-generation problem, and could be of independent interest to the community.

Reasonably thorough evaluation combining qualitative comparisons, quantitative embedding-similarity metrics, VBench-style fidelity metrics, and a fairly large-scale human preference study (669/455/252 annotations across three settings) with consistent, large win-rate margins over baselines.

The classifier-free guidance decomposition enabling separate control over reference-effect adherence and input-video adherence (Sec 4.5) is a nice practical extension that increases the method's usability.
Honest discussion of limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric dataset bias, inference cost) rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The 'tuning-free' framing in the title is somewhat inconsistent with the described training procedure, which fine-tunes a 14B parameter backbone with LoRA on a purpose-built dataset; the term appears to refer only to test-time behavior (no per-example optimization), but this could confuse readers and should be clarified up front.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of each of the three dataset sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V, code-based) to final model quality, nor ablations on architecture choices (e.g., width-wise vs channel-wise reference latent concatenation, mask design). This makes it hard to assess which components of the fairly complex data/model pipeline are actually necessary.

Much of the training data is itself synthetically generated by chaining several pretrained generative models (image generators, image editors, pose extractors, first-last-frame interpolators, GPT-4o for prompts), which risks compounding artifacts, distributional biases, and reduced fidelity to real-world effects; the paper does not analyze or quantify this risk (e.g., via manual quality audits beyond a brief filtering mention for V2V pairs).

Automatic quantitative metrics (VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity) are acknowledged by the authors themselves as only weakly correlated with actual task success, and the VBench-style fidelity metrics in the appendix show no clear differentiation between methods, leaving the human study as the only strong evidence of superiority—raising reproducibility/robustness concerns for future comparisons.

Validation sets are relatively small (56 I2V reference videos across 28 effects, ~100+ V2V pairs), which may limit the statistical reliability of the reported metrics and user-study conclusions given the diversity of effect types being claimed.
Code and dataset are not yet released (promised upon publication), limiting present reproducibility and independent verification of the dataset curation pipeline and claimed scale/diversity.

Baseline comparisons are inherently asymmetric (baselines only receive text prompts, since no other reference-conditioned baselines exist for this exact task), which is understandable given the paper's claim of introducing a new task, but it somewhat limits the strength of the 'outperforms baselines' claim since the comparison is more of an existence proof than a rigorous head-to-head against comparably-conditioned alternatives.

The paper's dataset is heavily skewed toward human-centric/foreground-dominant content (LoRA effects, Senorita human masks), which is acknowledged as a limitation but reduces the generality of the 'large-scale' and 'diverse' claims made in the abstract and contributions.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: transferring dynamic, time-varying visual effects from a reference video onto a separate target video/image, which existing prompt-based or keyframe-based editing methods cannot address.

Proposes a genuinely scalable, multi-source data curation pipeline (LoRA-based I2V, an automated V2V pipeline using first-last-frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects) that produces over 120K triplets spanning 1,700+ effects — a substantial engineering contribution that could be useful as a benchmark/dataset for future work.

The conditioning architecture extension of the Wan2.1 FLF2V backbone (width-wise latent concatenation of reference and input video tokens with a hybrid preservation mask) is clearly described and technically sound.

Comprehensive evaluation combining qualitative comparisons, a carefully designed large-scale human preference study (2AFC, practice trials, bootstrap confidence intervals, >15,000 annotations), and quantitative embedding-similarity and VBench-style metrics.
The multi-directional classifier-free guidance mechanism for controllable trade-off between input fidelity and effect adherence is a nice practical addition with qualitative demonstration.

Good transparency in limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, 2x inference cost) and detailed supplementary documentation of dataset/hyperparameters aiding reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: Reported human-preference win rates are relatively modest (roughly 53-67%), especially for I2V (56.8-57.4% RVA) — the text's framing of these as "large preference"/"strong preference" is somewhat overstated relative to the actual margins.

No baseline exists that can accept a reference video as conditioning, so all comparisons are against text-only methods; this makes the comparison somewhat structurally favorable to RefVFX and leaves open whether the gains stem from the reference-conditioning idea specifically or simply from having strictly more information (reference video) than baselines with only text.

Lack of ground-truth triplets for validation forces reliance on embedding similarity as a proxy, and the quantitative story is mixed: baselines sometimes score higher on input similarity, which the paper interprets favorably as "under-editing" but could equally indicate the proposed method over-edits or leaks reference-specific content; no metric to check whether effect is content-independent (a core stated challenge in the method).

VBench-style quality metrics (Table 10, aesthetic score, motion smoothness, dynamic degree) are comparable across all methods, which somewhat weakens the argument that RefVFX offers a clear quantitative advantage beyond the (contested) similarity metrics.
No ablations isolating the contribution of each of the three data sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V, code-based) to final model performance, despite this being a central claimed contribution.

The dataset construction pipeline depends heavily on several proprietary/closed models (Qwen-Image, Flux, GPT-4o, Wan2.1) for generating training pairs, which may hinder exact reproducibility even with code release.

"Tuning-free" in the title could be misleading, since the method requires large-scale supervised fine-tuning (LoRA on a 14B backbone) on a purpose-built dataset; the term is really only accurate with respect to test-time optimization, and this distinction is not clarified early enough.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: reference-based video temporal effect transfer, distinguishing itself clearly from prompt-based or keyframe-conditioned editing methods that cannot capture time-varying effects.

Proposes a comprehensive and scalable data curation pipeline combining three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V effects, a novel automated V2V pipeline using first-last frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects), yielding a large-scale dataset (120K+ triplets, 1700+ effects) that could be a valuable resource for the community.

The V2V triplet generation pipeline (Fig. 4) is a creative and non-trivial technical contribution addressing a real data scarcity problem, since naturally-occurring reference/input/output video triplets do not exist.

Reasonable architectural design that extends the Wan2.1 FLF2V conditioning scheme to jointly incorporate reference effect video and input video via width-wise latent concatenation, with a sensible hybrid masking scheme.

Extensive evaluation combining qualitative results, quantitative embedding similarity metrics, and a large-scale human preference study (15,000+ annotations, 500+ annotators) with reasonable statistical treatment (bootstrap CIs).
Additional controllability analysis (dual classifier-free guidance over reference and input video) is a nice practical feature enabling user control at inference time.

The paper is transparent about limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, inference cost) and provides substantial supplementary detail (dataset composition, user study protocol, extended quantitative metrics).
weaknesses: The reported win rates in the human preference study are fairly modest (mostly 53-67%, often close to the 50% chance baseline, e.g., I2V RVA at 56.8-57.4%), which somewhat undercuts the claim of the method 'consistently' and 'largely' outperforming baselines; some deltas are within or near one standard deviation of chance.

Quantitative VBench-style metrics (Table 10, aesthetic/motion/dynamic degree) show the method is roughly comparable to or sometimes worse than baselines (e.g., lower dynamic degree in some settings), and this is not discussed critically in the main text.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of each of the three dataset sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V pipeline, code-based effects) to final model performance, making it hard to assess which data source drives most of the gains.

No ablation on the proposed conditioning/architecture design (e.g., alternative fusion mechanisms, effect of the hybrid mask, or removing width-wise reference concatenation) beyond the single 'No Ref' baseline, limiting insight into why the specific architectural choices were made.

The automated V2V data pipeline is complex and depends on multiple pretrained components (image generator, image editor, pose extractor, conditional video generator); potential compounding of errors/artifacts across this pipeline and their downstream impact on training data quality is not quantitatively analyzed.

Reliance on VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity as the primary quantitative proxy for effect transfer quality is acknowledged as imperfect by the authors themselves, but no additional automatic metric (e.g., an effect-specific classifier or a video-language model-based judge) is used to corroborate results beyond human study.

The paper does not report evaluation on truly out-of-distribution effect categories beyond 'unseen' variants of similar effect types already represented in the training taxonomy (human-centric, stylistic transformations, weather effects), so generalization claims to genuinely novel effect classes are not strongly substantiated.
Code and full dataset release is only promised ('will be released upon publication'), so reproducibility currently cannot be independently verified by reviewers.

The paper title/abstract claims 'tuning-free' but the method requires substantial LoRA fine-tuning of a 14B parameter backbone for 10K steps, which is a training-time cost; the 'tuning-free' framing refers only to inference-time behavior and could be clarified to avoid confusion with typical zero-shot 'tuning-free' methods in prior literature.
